note: Invented pilot histories for the Squadron Room. Every route below is a real way a man reached a fighter cockpit by the summer of 1940, and every school, unit and place named is real and was doing that job at that time. The men are invented. A story is the route's paragraphs followed by the side's closing paragraph. Tokens in {braces} are either computed ({first}, {last}, {name}, {born}, {year}, {age}, {place}, {joined}, {type}, {unit}, {base}, and on the British side {posted}, {hours}, {ontype}, {otu}) or are looked up in the side's lists, one item picked by a number made from the pilot's name, so the same man gets the same past every time, and the same item is reused if a token appears twice in one story. List items may themselves contain tokens. Rules for anyone adding to the lists: family items stay neutral about the birthplace; only the father lists mention a father, only the sibling list mentions brothers or sisters, and the mother is always alive; every item must read correctly in every sentence that uses its token. Check any change with dev/render_backgrounds.py. Read by Get-PilotBackground in BOB2_SquadronRoom.ps1.

father: His father came back from the Western Front in 1919 and never spoke of it.
His father drove an engine on the railway, and his mother kept a small shop in the front room.
His father, an elementary schoolmaster, would have kept him at school longer had there been the money.
His father had been a rigger in the Royal Flying Corps, and kept a splintered piece of propeller on the mantelpiece.
His father kept a chemist's shop, and the family lived over it.
His father, a works foreman, held that a job was done properly or not at all.
His father died in 1924 of his war wounds, and his mother brought him up on a pension and her dressmaking.
His father was a postman who grew prize chrysanthemums, and his mother played the organ at chapel.
His father drove a brewery van, and had taught him to drive it by the time he was fourteen.
His father was a compositor at a printing works, a careful man with ink under his nails.
fatheroff: His father was a doctor, whose patients came to the side door at all hours.
His father, a solicitor, had a place waiting for him in the firm and was patient about it.
His father was a clergyman with a small stipend and a large library.
His father had been a gunner officer in the last war and afterwards managed a branch of a bank.
His father was a civil engineer, abroad for years at a time building harbours, and known chiefly by his letters.
His father, a regular soldier, had retired as a major and taken to gardening with military thoroughness.
His father owned a small engineering business and assumed that his son would come into it.
His father died when he was small and is chiefly a photograph on the piano; an uncle paid the school fees.
His father was a schoolmaster who taught classics and distrusted machinery.
His father edited a provincial newspaper, and the house was full of proofs and argument.
sibling: There were three children, of whom he was the eldest.
One sister, four years older, taught him to read before he went to school.
Two younger sisters thought him a great bore until he came home in uniform.
A younger brother followed him everywhere, and follows him still by post.
The youngest of four, he was used to waiting his turn.
An elder brother went into the Navy, which settled where the younger would not go.
Of three boys he was the middle one, and the one who could not sit still.
pastime: As a boy he built wireless sets from parts bought with his pocket money.
He sang treble in the church choir until his voice broke.
From the age of twelve he kept the scorebook for a cricket club, in a hand neater than the secretary's.
His boyhood was spent on a bicycle, which he took to pieces and rebuilt every winter.
Cigarette cards of aeroplanes were his passion, and he knew every type in the set by its outline.
A keen Boy Scout, he was a good one mostly because he liked maps.
He read everything in the public library that had an engine in it.
Football and cricket filled his boyhood, and he claims to have been picked for neither on merit.
His holidays were spent in a garage, handing spanners to a mechanic who let him watch.
Good with his hands, he made model aeroplanes of balsa and tissue, most of which flew once.
spark: When he was fourteen a touring air circus came to the town, and five shillings bought him ten minutes in an old Avro.
At an air display when he was fourteen he stood at the rope from the first take-off to the last landing.
What settled it was a silver biplane fighter seen from a train, keeping pace for a mile before it rolled away.
Every week he bought a flying magazine, read it from cover to cover, and filed it in order under his bed.
On his fifteenth birthday a family friend who had flown in the last war took him up and let him hold the stick.
From the age of ten he cycled out to the nearest aerodrome to lie in the grass by the boundary and watch.
The Schneider Trophy races filled the newspapers, and he cut out the photographs of the seaplanes and pinned them over his bed.
Where the wish to fly came from he could never say, only that it was there by the time he was twelve.
solo: He went solo after nine hours. His instructor climbed out one dull afternoon, fastened the straps across the empty seat, and told him not to bend it.
His first solo landing was really three, one after another down the field. When he taxied in the instructor was lighting his pipe and seemed not to have been watching.
He was slow to go solo because he would not leave the controls alone. Aeroplanes, his instructor told him, had flown perfectly well before he was born.
On his first solo the aeroplane, lighter by one instructor, climbed so fast that he was at a thousand feet before he had stopped talking to himself.
He went solo in eight hours, the first of his course, and it went to his head for a week, until a crosswind landing took it out again.
The first solo came on a still evening after ten hours of dual. He flew one circuit, landed, and sat for a full minute before taxiing in.
His instructor, a man with a bad back and no small talk, sent him solo with the remark that he was unlikely to improve by being watched.
His first solo he remembers less well than the flight before it, when he bounced so badly that the instructor took over without a word.
moment: On a night cross-country he lost himself for twenty minutes, found a railway line shining under the moon and followed it home. He told nobody.
He once came in to land with the wheels still up and was saved by the warning horn. His instructor never mentioned it again, which was worse than a lecture.
An instructor wrote that he flew accurately and landed as if the ground owed him money. He worked at his landings for a month, and they improved.
In his second week he swung on landing and took off a wing tip. His flight commander walked the skid mark with him, slowly, and then sent him straight up again.
Instrument flying under the hood nearly finished him. He passed the test at the second attempt, and remains a little proud of how much he disliked it.
Formation flying came easily to him and aerobatics did not. His slow rolls, an instructor told him, were neither.
On his first night solo the flare path vanished under the nose on the approach, as he had been warned it would, and he went round twice before he landed.
Halfway through the course an instructor told him that he would make a sound pilot if he stopped trying to be a brilliant one. He wrote it in his log book.
temper: In the air he is careful rather than dashing, and is always where he ought to be.
His assessments say above the average as a pilot and average as a shot, and he thinks both about right.
In the mess he is quiet; after a flight he talks, and cannot help going over every minute of it.
People find him easy company. He listens more than he talks, laughs readily, and is slow to take offence.
There is a stubborn streak in him that his instructors noted and his friends work around.
Nobody would call him a natural pilot, and he knows it. What he has is application.
Steadier than his years and a little solemn, he is someone the others have taken to asking things.
His flying is smooth and his landings neat, and he is chiefly afraid of making a fool of himself.
He is cheerful in the mornings, which is held against him.
Not a great talker, he does what he is asked, does it properly, and keeps his opinions to himself.
habit: Before every flight he walks round his aeroplane with his hands in his pockets, looking at everything and touching nothing.
A neat upright hand fills his log book, and the lines are ruled in red ink.
A pipe that is forever going out and a sixpenny paperback travel in his tunic pockets.
Before a flight he polishes his own windscreen, however clean it already is.
Sleep comes to him anywhere, at once, and leaves the moment the dispersal telephone rings.
On the mess piano he plays by ear, the same five tunes, and is always asked for a sixth.
In the evenings he rides a bicycle round the perimeter track, for something to do with his legs.
When he is concentrating he whistles through his teeth, and has no idea that he does it.
A friend from school plays chess with him by post, a move a week, and is winning.
Lately he has been teaching himself to draw, and the margins of his letters are full of aeroplanes.
home: His mother writes every Sunday, and he answers every Sunday, saying very little about flying.
There is a girl at home, Joan, who writes twice a week and to whom he is not quite engaged.
At home his room is as he left it, books and all, and his mother dusts it on Fridays.
Part of his pay goes home every month, and he has mentioned it to no one.
A motor cycle, bought second-hand with his first pay, stands under a sheet in the shed at home.
At home an elderly dog still goes to the gate at the hour he used to come in.
His mother keeps his letters in a biscuit tin and still addresses hers to Master {first} {last}.
Since the war began he has been home once, for four days, and spent most of them asleep.
On his last leave the house seemed smaller, and he found little to say about what he did.

text: {name} was born on {born} in {place}. {father} {pastime} From {school} he went, at sixteen, to work as {job}.

{spark} Private flying cost more for an hour than he earned in a week, but the Volunteer Reserve taught young men to fly at weekends and at the public expense, and in {joined} it took him as an airman under training, pilot. Civilian instructors at {erfts} taught him on the Tiger Moth and later the Hawker Hart.

{solo} Called up with the rest of the Reserve on 1 September 1939, he waited some weeks for a course. {itw} gave him drill and ground subjects; {sfts} gave him {trainer}, his wings and a Sergeant's stripes. At {otu} the {type} took about a fortnight, with hardly a round fired, and he left with some {hours} hours in all.
{temper} {habit} {home}
{name} comes from {place}, where he was born on {born}. {father} {pastime}

{spark} For a boy without money the way into the Air Force was an aircraft apprenticeship, and at sixteen he left {school} for No. 1 School of Technical Training, Halton. Three years later he passed out in the trade of {trade}. {last} worked on aeroplanes and watched other men fly them until {joined}, when he was chosen for pilot training from the ranks, as a few ex-apprentices were each year.

He began again at the bottom, as a pupil, and went on to {trainer} at {sfts}. {moment} Wings and a Sergeant's stripes came together. The {type} he learned at {otu}: about a fortnight, very little firing, and a Merlin engine he would have liked longer to look at.
{last} knows what is under the cowling better than most officers, and the ground crew listen to him. {temper} {habit} {home}
{name} was born on {born} in {place}. {fatheroff} {pastime} School was {pubschool}.

{spark} In {joined} he answered an Air Ministry advertisement for short service commissions: four years on the active list and six on the reserve. His first flying was done as a civilian at {civschool}, under contract to the Air Ministry. Then came a fortnight of drill and tailors at the RAF Depot, Uxbridge, and his name in the Gazette as an Acting Pilot Officer on probation.
At {sfts} he flew {trainer}. {moment} In due course he took his wings and was posted to fighters. The {type} he learned at {otu}, where the course ran to about a fortnight and very little gunnery.
What {last} will do when the commission runs out he has not decided, and the question has stopped being asked. {temper} {habit} {home}
{name} was born on {born} and brought up in {place}. {fatheroff} {sibling} {pastime} His school was {pubschool}.

{spark} The Air Force was to be his career, and that meant the Royal Air Force College at Cranwell. He sat the competitive examination and entered as a flight cadet in {joined}. The two years there gave as much time to the parade ground, the lecture room and the sports field as to the air.

The flying was done on the Avro Tutor and then the Hawker Hart. {solo} A permanent commission followed. The College closed to cadets at the outbreak of war, and the course he took is no longer given. The {type} he learned at {otu}, in about a fortnight.
A regular officer among men who mostly are not, {last} is expected to know the book, and does. {temper} {habit} {home}
{name} comes from {place}, where he was born on {born}. {fatheroff} {sibling} {pastime} From {pubschool} he {univ}.

{spark} At university the Air Squadron was the obvious next step. It flew Avro Tutors, taught undergraduates to fly for nothing, and asked only that they turn up, which he did more faithfully than he went to lectures. In {joined} he was commissioned in the Volunteer Reserve.

Called up in September 1939, he found that the Air Force meant to teach him again from the beginning. {itw} supplied the drill, and {sfts} supplied {trainer} and, in the end, his wings. {moment} At {otu} the {type} took about a fortnight, and he left with some {hours} hours in all.
The degree is unfinished, and {last} does not seem to miss it. {temper} {habit} {home}

father: His father served in the artillery from 1914 to 1918 and came home with a limp and little to say.
His father was a master baker, and it was understood that the shop would one day be his.
His father, a railway official, lost his savings in the inflation of 1923, and the family lived carefully ever after.
His father had been an observer in a two-seater in 1917 and kept the photographs in a drawer.
His father taught at the elementary school and was strict at home in the same even way.
His father died when he was small, and he was brought up by his mother and an uncle.
His father drove a tram and knew half the district by name.
His father was a cabinet maker, and the flat always smelled of glue and wood shavings.
His father was a foreman in a machine factory and came home at the same minute every evening.
His father kept a small inn, where the boy was carrying glasses before he could see over the bar.
fatheroff: His father was a doctor, whose surgery took up the ground floor of the family house.
His father had been an infantry officer in the war and was afterwards a discontented official of an insurance company.
His father was a judge at the district court, a precise and kindly man.
His father taught Latin and Greek at a Gymnasium across the town and had hoped for a scholar.
His father was an engineer with a firm that built bridges, and was often away.
His father had flown as an observer in 1917 and kept the photographs in a drawer, to be looked at on Sundays.
His father died in 1925, and his mother let rooms to students to keep him at school.
His father owned a small printing works and would have liked a son in the business.
His father was a senior official of the postal service, a man of fixed habits.
His father was a regular officer, retired in 1920 when the army was cut down, who never quite found another occupation.
sibling: There were four children, of whom he was the eldest.
A younger brother is still at school.
Of three sons he was the second.
There was one sister, two years younger, his ally in everything.
The youngest of five, he was mostly left to himself.
pastime: As a boy he kept goal for a football club and was good enough to be noticed.
He read whatever he could find, adventure stories above all, and was teased for it.
Model gliders of pine strip and paper were his passion, and most of them were lost over the neighbours' roofs.
A good gymnast, small and quick, he won a district medal that his mother still keeps.
His free afternoons were spent at a rowing club on the river.
He took bicycles and clocks apart, and got most of them together again.
Summers were spent with grandparents in the country, where he learned to milk a cow and drive a horse.
He sang in a church choir until his voice broke.
He swam for his school and claims to have disliked every length.
He drew well, aeroplanes and ships for the most part, in the margins of his school books.
glidebit: The first launch gave him eleven seconds in the air, a hop down the slope on a rubber rope and a landing on the skid.
For every minute in the air there was an hour of hauling the glider back up the hill, which he thought a fair exchange.
The A certificate asked for a straight glide of thirty seconds, and he managed thirty-four.
The group built its own glider one winter, and he glued ribs for four months before he was allowed to sit in it.
On his fourth launch he broke a skid, and he spent the rest of that summer repairing it.
An instructor there, who had flown in the war and said little, taught him to feel the air through the seat of his trousers.
moment: His first powered solo came after some fifty circuits with an instructor who shouted down the speaking tube throughout. The silence, he says, was the strangest part.
On his first solo cross-country he mistook one town for another, landed in a meadow to ask a farmer the way, and took off again before anyone could report him.
A heavy landing cost him a bent undercarriage leg and three days confined to barracks. He has been gentle with aeroplanes ever since.
Aerobatics were the first thing in his life that he had been plainly better at than everyone around him, and he took care not to say so.
His instructor told him that he flew like a glider pilot, too gently and too politely, and that the engine was there to be used.
Airsick on his first three powered flights, he said nothing. On the fourth it stopped, and it has not returned.
When his engine failed on a cross-country flight he put the trainer down in a stubble field without a scratch, as any glider pilot would.
Instrument flying came hard to him. Under the hood he once flew a gentle spiral that he would have sworn was level flight.
funkmoment: By the end of the course he could read Morse faster than he could write it down, which the instructors said was the usual complaint.
On his first air firing detail he put most of a drum into empty air and a few rounds into the drogue, and was told that this was about average.
Airsick on his first training flights, he learned to take down a message with a paper bag on his knee.
His first direction finding exercise in the air put the aircraft forty kilometres from where it was. He had taken a bearing the wrong way round.
His section instructor held that a wireless operator who could not change a valve in the dark with gloves on was a passenger.
He passed out near the top of his course in Morse and near the bottom in gunnery, and has worked at the second ever since.
whyfly: because the flying pay was worth having
because a friend from the barrack room did and he would not be left behind
because he had never been in an aeroplane and wanted to know what it was like
for no better reason, he says, than boredom with the parade ground
because the alternative was a telephone exchange in a cellar
because an instructor told him that he would never pass the medical
war: He reached the Gruppe in time for the campaign in the West, and flew over Belgium and northern France.
He came too late for the fighting in France, and has fired his guns only at targets.
He flew through the campaign in the West in May and June 1940, escort work mostly, and ended it without a claim.
He arrived from the replacement pool in June 1940, as the fighting in France was ending, and has still to prove himself.
temper: Calm in the air and economical with words, he is marked down by his Staffelkapitän as reliable.
In the air he is quick and a little impatient; on the ground he is slow to anger and hard to dislike.
His flying is tidy rather than brilliant, and he still looks at the sky first, as glider pilots do.
Those who fly with him say that he is easy to follow and does nothing sudden without a reason.
Ambitious in a quiet way, he keeps it to himself and works at his gunnery more than most.
There is a dry humour in him that new acquaintances take some time to notice.
Conscientious to a fault, he is the kind of man who reads the handbook twice and then asks the mechanics.
Sociable and a good mimic, he is more serious about his flying than he allows anyone to see.
crewtemper: A steady man in the back seat, unhurried on the key and sparing with the intercom, he is never asked twice whether a message has gone.
His reports over the intercom are short and exact: what, where, how far. His pilot says it is like flying with a good clock.
On the ground he is the more talkative half of the crew, and in the air the quieter.
The set is his own affair: he trusts nobody else's soldering, and is on good terms with the signals section in spite of it.
Watching the sky backwards is not something he pretends to enjoy, only to be good at.
Pilot and wireless operator are unlike in most things and have found that it does not matter.
habit: He plays the accordion, badly, and is asked to anyway.
Every spare minute goes to reading, and his kit is heavier than anyone's by the weight of the books.
On free afternoons he keeps goal for the Staffel football team.
He carves model aeroplanes from whatever wood the carpenters will give him, and gives them away.
With his first pay he bought a camera, and he has filled two albums since the spring.
Most evenings he plays Skat for small stakes, and wins more often than chance would explain.
By his own account he smokes too much, and he gives it up on the first of every month.
Wherever he goes a diary goes too, a few lines a day, most of them about the weather.
Up before anyone else, he is usually to be found with the mechanics, drinking their coffee.
Whenever he is working at something he whistles, tunelessly.
home: He writes to his mother every week, and to a girl in his home town rather less often than she would like.
His mother sends parcels of cake that arrive as crumbs, and he writes to thank her for every one.
His fiancée, Anneliese, he has known since school, and her photograph travels in his pay book.
His last leave was at Christmas, and he spent most of it asleep or eating.
His mother's letters begin 'My dear {first}' and end with instructions to dress warmly, whatever the season.
Half his pay goes home, and he has told nobody.
It is a long time since he was last at home, and he says that the town will keep.
A motor cycle that he had half paid for stands in a shed at home.

text: {name} was born on {born} in {place}. {father} {pastime} School was {school}, and after it came {job}.

Powered flying was forbidden to Germany by the Treaty of Versailles when he was a boy, and like thousands of others he came to the air by glider. {last} learned to glide {glide}. {glidebit} The A, B and C certificates followed, and after six months in the Reich Labour Service he was called up in {joined} and accepted by the Luftwaffe for aircrew.

Recruit training with a Fliegerausbildungsregiment came first, months of drill and no aeroplane. Then came {ab}, and the A and B licences on the Focke-Wulf Stieglitz, the Bücker Jungmann and the Arado 66. {moment} Selected for fighters, he went to {jfs}, flew the Arado 68 and the early Bf 109, and reached the front through the Ergänzungsjagdgruppe at Merseburg.
{war} {temper} {habit} {home}
{name} comes from {place}, where he was born on {born}. {fatheroff} {sibling} {pastime} His school was {gymnasium}.

He was a glider pilot before he was anything else. Powered flying was still forbidden to Germany when he was a schoolboy, and his holidays were spent {glide}. {glidebit} After his Abitur and six months in the Reich Labour Service he entered the Luftwaffe in {joined} as a Fahnenjunker, an officer candidate.

The service sent him to {lks}, where infantry drill, tactics, air law and flying training ran side by side and ended in the officer's examination and the pilot's badge. {moment} The fighter course followed at {jfs}, on the Arado 68 and the early marks of the Bf 109, and with it his commission as Leutnant.
{war} {temper} {habit} {home}
{name} was born on {born} and grew up in {place}. {father} {pastime} Schooling meant {school}, and it led to {job}.

Flying, for a German boy of those years, meant gliding, since powered aircraft were forbidden to the country by treaty. {last} first left the ground {glide}. {glidebit} Six months in the Reich Labour Service followed, and then the call-up. In {joined} the Luftwaffe accepted him for aircrew.

After recruit training came {ab} and the A and B licences. {moment} At fighter school he did well enough to be picked for the Zerstörer arm, which then had its choice of the best pupils. That meant a longer road than the single-seat men took: the C school for multi-engined aircraft, a blind flying course, and at last the Zerstörerschule at Schleißheim and a Bf 110 with a wireless operator behind him.
{war} {temper} {habit} {home}
{name} was born on {born} in {place}. {fatheroff} {sibling} {pastime} School was {gymnasium}.

Like most pilots of his age he began on gliders, powered flying being forbidden to Germany when he was at school. His gliding was done {glide}. {glidebit} In {joined}, with his Abitur and six months of Reich Labour Service behind him, he entered the Luftwaffe as an officer candidate and was sent to {lks}.

There he was drilled as an infantryman, taught tactics and air law, and taught to fly, all more or less at once. {moment} Commissioned, and with his pilot's badge, he asked for fighters and was given the Zerstörer, for which the best pupils were then being chosen. The C school for multi-engined aircraft and a blind flying course followed, and then the Zerstörerschule at Schleißheim.
{war} {temper} {habit} {home}
{name} was born on {born} in {place}. {father} {sibling} {pastime} School was {school}, and after it came {radiojob}.

Flying had no part in his plans. After six months in the Reich Labour Service he was called up in {joined}, and the Luftwaffe, seeing his trade, put him down for signals. When volunteers were asked for as aircrew he gave in his name, {whyfly}.

At {lns} he learned Morse at speed, the FuG 10 set, direction finding, and air gunnery with the MG 15 on its flexible mount. {funkmoment} At the Zerstörerschule at Schleißheim he was crewed with a pilot, more or less by lot, and the two have flown together since.
In a Bf 110 the wireless operator sits facing aft. {last} works the radio, watches the sky behind, and has one rifle-calibre machine gun with which to keep it clear. {crewtemper} {habit} {home}
